guideTitle: Best Printers for iPhone and iPad (2026)
metaTitle: Best Printers for iPhone and iPad in 2026
metaDescription: Six printers that work well with iPhone and iPad through AirPrint or a free app, from tank inkjets to pocket photo printers, with setup and cost advice.
expertTake: The Canon PIXMA TR4720 is the best overall pick for iPhone and iPad owners because it prints, scans and copies over Wi-Fi with AirPrint and no driver. The Canon PIXMA TS5320 is the value pick for a small household that prints a few pages a week. If photos are the only reason you print, a pocket dye-sublimation photo printer is cheaper than any all-in-one.
introParagraphs: Printing from an iPhone or iPad should be the easy part, since Apple built a driverless protocol into iOS and iPadOS. The harder questions are which printers support it cleanly, how much their ink costs, and whether you want documents, photos or both.

Most households print a mix of school forms, boarding passes and the occasional photo. A general all-in-one covers the first two, and a small thermal photo printer handles the third far better than an office machine, so the right buy depends on how you split your printing.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer with ADF
products.description:
The TR4720 is a compact four-in-one with an auto document feeder, built for people who print from a phone or tablet. AirPrint support means an iPhone or iPad finds it on the Wi-Fi network and prints without installing a driver, and the Canon PRINT app adds scanning and settings. That combination makes first-time setup quick.

The compromise is the cartridge ink system. Running cost per page is higher than on a tank model such as the Epson ET-2800, so it suits a household that prints in moderation. Against the TS5320, the TR4720 adds the document feeder and fax, which helps if you scan forms and send them from your phone.

Ownership is easy: the cartridges snap in, the body is small, and the paper tray holds enough for weekly use. Print a page every couple of weeks so the printhead stays clear, and keep the iPhone on the same network when you add the printer. If your phone cannot see it after a router change, restart the printer and the router before reinstalling anything. A parent who scans permission slips can use the feeder to capture a full stack in one pass and email it from the phone. Over a year, the main recurring cost is cartridges, so check the larger XL size at purchase, since it lowers cost per page for anyone printing weekly rather than monthly.
products.bestFor: Households that print and scan from an iPhone or iPad every week.
pros: AirPrint finds it without a driver
Auto document feeder for scanning stacks
Fax included for the odd form
Small body fits on a shelf
cons: Cartridge ink costs more per page

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2800 Wireless Color All-in-One Supertank
products.description:
The ET-2800 is an ink tank all-in-one with flatbed scanning and Wi-Fi, so an iPhone or iPad can print through AirPrint or the Epson Smart Panel app. It fills from bottles instead of cartridges, which is why a family that prints regularly will spend far less on ink than with the cartridge Canons.

It trades a faster, more featured body for that economy. There is no document feeder and no automatic duplex, so scanning a stack means placing each page on the glass. Compared with the Canon TR4720, you gain ink savings and lose the feeder and fax.

In ownership, fill the tanks slowly and print something weekly so the ink does not dry in the printhead. The body is bigger than the Canons because of the tanks, but it still sits happily on a desk. Keep the iPhone and printer on the same Wi-Fi band, since a 2.4 GHz only printer can fail to appear if the phone is on a different network. The Epson Smart Panel app also lets you check ink levels and start a scan from the phone, which is handy when the printer sits in another room. The ink bottles are keyed so each color only fits its own tank, which removes the most common refill mistake and makes the first fill an unhurried job.
products.bestFor: Families that print a lot from phones and tablets and want low ink cost.
pros: Refillable tanks cut cost per page

products.name: Brother Work Smart 1360 Wireless Color Inkjet All-in-One
products.description:
The Work Smart 1360 offers automatic duplex printing, a 20-sheet feeder and scanning to cloud services such as Google Drive and Dropbox. For an iPad user who scans documents to the cloud rather than to a computer, that workflow is smoother than on a basic printer.

It costs more than the entry Canons and still uses cartridges, so running cost sits above the Epson tank. The reward is two-sided printing, which saves paper for long documents and school packets.

Owners should keep paper stored flat to avoid duplex jams and clear the feeder of staples. A compact footprint makes it easy to keep on a bookshelf next to an iPad charging stand. Print weekly so the cartridges do not dry out, and use the Brother app to check ink levels from the phone. Scanning to the cloud from an iPad is the standout use, because you can capture a receipt or a signed form and file it in a folder without touching a computer. If you often print thick packets, the duplex path saves paper, and the 20-sheet feeder is enough for most household scans, though it will not suit a bulky archive project.
products.bestFor: Home office users who scan to the cloud and print two-sided from an iPad.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS5320 All-in-One Wireless Printer with AirPrint
products.description:
The TS5320 is a compact all-in-one with a small OLED display and a two-cartridge system. AirPrint support means an iPhone prints to it with no driver, and the simple two-cartridge layout makes replacement easy.

It is an older design, so features are modest. Compared with the TR4720, it lacks the document feeder and fax, and compared with the Epson ET-2800, it costs more to run. Its charm is the low price and the small size.

A household that prints a few pages a week will find it fine. Keep it near the router, print a page every couple of weeks, and watch the ink levels on the OLED display. It is not the machine for a student printing papers every night, because cartridge costs add up quickly. The small OLED display shows ink and network status at a glance, which spares you from digging through a phone app when something goes wrong. For a grandparent or a first-time owner, the plain button layout and short setup are an advantage, since there is little to get lost in.
products.bestFor: Small households printing a few pages a week from a phone.

products.name: Liene Amber M110 Bluetooth Portable Photo Printer with Two Paper Sizes
products.description:
The Amber M110 is a portable photo printer that connects by Bluetooth and prints 4 by 6 inch and 3 by 3 inch photos using thermal dye-sublimation. The process lays down smooth color and finishes with a protective coat, so prints come out dry and ready to handle.

It only prints photos, so it does not replace an all-in-one for documents. Next to the Liene M100, it adds Bluetooth and a dual paper tray, and the trade is a limited media supply because it uses the maker's paper and ribbon kits.

It is small enough to keep in a drawer and use at a party or a family event. Store the paper kits sealed and away from heat, keep the phone app updated, and print a test photo before an event. A kit prints a fixed number of photos, so count the cost per print before you commit. The dual paper tray lets you switch between standard 4 by 6 prints and small square prints without swapping sheets, which is handy for photo walls and scrapbook pages. Since Bluetooth pairing is per phone, set up each family device once and delete old pairings that clutter the app.
products.bestFor: People who print photos from an iPhone and want a pocket sized machine.

products.name: Liene M100 4x6 Wi-Fi Photo Printer with Built-In Hotspot
products.description:
The M100 prints 4 by 6 inch photos and creates its own Wi-Fi hotspot, so a phone connects directly without a home router. It uses thermal dye-sublimation for continuous tone color and ships with sheets and cartridges to start.

The tradeoff against the Amber M110 is the connection: the hotspot means your phone temporarily leaves your home network while it prints, which is awkward but works anywhere. It is a single-size printer and only handles photos.

Owners should keep paper sealed and store the machine flat. Because the printer is a photo specialist, treat it as a companion to an office printer rather than a replacement for one. Print a test image first, and replace the cartridge when the app warns it is low. At a birthday party or a campsite, the hotspot approach is its best trick, because nobody has to share a password and the printer works even with no internet at all. At home, though, the Bluetooth Amber is the smoother daily choice, since your phone stays on the household network and can still browse while printing.
products.bestFor: Family events and travel where no router is available.
cons: Phone leaves home Wi-Fi while printing

buyingCriteria.explanation: AirPrint is Apple's driverless protocol, so a compatible printer appears in the iPhone or iPad print menu with no app. The Canon TR4720, TS5320 and Epson ET-2800 all support it. Check the listing for AirPrint rather than assuming, because a few cheap printers support only a vendor app.

Many home printers use 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only, which can fail to appear if your phone is on a different band or a guest network. Keep the phone and printer on the same network during setup. A printer with a USB fallback helps if the router misbehaves.

Cartridge printers such as the Canon TS5320 are cheap to buy and costly to run, while the Epson ET-2800 uses ink bottles and costs far less per page. If you print more than about 100 pages a month, tanks win. For occasional use, a cartridge printer is fine.

An all-in-one like the Canon TR4720 handles forms and boarding passes, but a pocket dye-sublimation printer such as the Liene Amber M110 gives better small photos. Many households end up owning one of each. Decide which job matters most.

Phone scanning apps work well for single pages, but a document feeder is faster for stacks. The Canon TR4720 and Brother Work Smart 1360 include feeders, while the Epson ET-2800 uses the glass only. Choose based on how many documents you scan.
A portable photo printer fits in a drawer, while a tank printer needs a desk. The Liene M100 and Amber M110 are small, and the ET-2800 is the bulkiest here. Measure the spot before you buy.

howWeEvaluated.title: Apple compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated how easily each printer works with iOS and iPadOS, based on AirPrint support and app availability. Driverless printing scored highest. Photo printers that rely on an app scored lower for documents.

howWeEvaluated.title: Running cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cartridge and tank economics. The Epson ET-2800 led on cost, and cartridge models such as the TS5320 trailed. Photo printers were judged on cost per print.

howWeEvaluated.title: Document features
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed feeders, duplex and scanning options. The TR4720 and Brother 1360 scored well, while the ET-2800 lacks a feeder. This follows the spec sheet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup simplicity
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how smooth network setup is for a phone owner. Models with a clear app and a USB fallback scored higher. Owner feedback patterns often mention Wi-Fi band confusion.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared size and power needs. Pocket photo printers such as the Liene Amber M110 scored high for travel, and tank printers scored lower.

cards.label: Ink tank
cards.text: The Epson ET-2800 costs more at purchase and far less per page. It suits regular printers.

cards.label: Cartridge
cards.text: The Canon TR4720, TS5320 and Brother 1360 cost less upfront and more in ink. They suit moderate use.

howToChoose.note: Regular printers choose the tank, light users choose cartridges.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for AirPrint, cloud scanning and a clear app. An iPad often replaces a laptop, so the printer should work without a computer.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Canon TR4720 and Brother Work Smart 1360 are the strongest, since both scan to the phone or cloud and print driverlessly.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Step up if you print weekly or need duplex and a feeder, which points to the Brother 1360 or the Epson ET-2800.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you print rarely, where the Canon TS5320 is enough.

maintenance.why: Idle nozzles dry out. A short print keeps ink flowing.

maintenance.task: Keep printer and phone on one network
maintenance.why: A changed network or band hides the printer from AirPrint. Re-join and restart.
Updates fix connection bugs. Keep the iOS version current too.
Humidity and heat damage dye-sublimation media. Keep kits flat and dry.
Dust reduces grip. A damp lint-free cloth restores feeding.

faq.q: Do I need an app to print from an iPhone?
faq.a: Not with AirPrint. The Canon TR4720, TS5320 and Epson ET-2800 appear in the print menu on their own. Photo printers usually need their own app.

faq.q: Why can't my iPhone find my printer?
faq.a: Usually the phone and printer are on different Wi-Fi bands or networks. Join them to the same network and restart both before reinstalling anything.

faq.q: Is a tank printer worth it?
faq.a: If you print regularly, yes. The Epson ET-2800 costs far less per page than cartridge models, though it needs regular use.

faq.q: Can I scan from my iPad?
faq.a: Yes. Printers with a manufacturer app, such as Canon and Epson, scan to the device, and the Brother 1360 scans to cloud services.
Dye-sublimation machines like the Liene Amber M110 produce smooth, dry prints. They cost more per photo than an inkjet but need no ink maintenance.

faq.q: Which is best for school forms?
faq.a: A compact all-in-one such as the Canon TR4720 handles forms, scans and boarding passes with AirPrint and a feeder.
